### The original feed-forward neural language model ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/neural-lm-bengio-2026-11-03/bengio-original-figure1.png|Original Bengio neural language model: shared word lookup, tanh, softmax and optional direct connections]] *Yoshua Bengio, Réjean Ducharme, Pascal Vincent and Christian Jauvin, [Figure 1, A Neural Probabilistic Language Model](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf#page=6), JMLR 3 (2003), p.1142. Complete original diagram and caption, rendered from the publisher PDF; no labels redrawn. Author copyright ©2003. [JMLR publication policy and reuse note](/licenses/bengio03a-figure1-jmlr-policy.txt).* Read the figure from the word indices at the bottom. Each index selects a row of the same matrix $C$; the three lookup positions do not own three separate embedding tables. The selected vectors form the input to a tanh hidden layer. The output layer produces one score per vocabulary word, then softmax normalizes the scores. The dashed green paths bypass the hidden layer. In the paper's notation, the unnormalized output vector is $$ y=b+Wx+U\tanh(d+Hx). $$ Here $x$ concatenates the selected word vectors. The direct matrix $W$ is optional: setting it to zero leaves the hidden-layer route used by `WindowLM` below. The paper's $y$ corresponds to this chapter's logits $z$, not to a target token ID. Its $W$ is also not the output matrix called $W$ in our earlier bigram calculation. For the `WindowLM` dimensions used at the end of the chapter, the correspondence is: | Paper | `WindowLM` parameter | Shape | |---|---|---| | $C$ | `embedding.weight` | $8\times2$ | | $H,d$ | `network[0].weight`, `.bias` | $8\times4$, $8$ | | $U,b$ | `network[2].weight`, `.bias` | $8\times8$, $8$ | | Optional $W$ | No direct path in this implementation | $8\times4$ if added | The hidden-layer-only version has 128 parameters, as counted in the training example. Adding the direct $W$ would add 32 weights and change the model. The source annotation “most computation here” concerns its large-vocabulary output layer; the diagram alone does not measure the runtime of our eight-token example. ### Context order and repeated lookups The paper writes its concatenation from the newest context word to the oldest. `WindowLM` constructs windows in chronological order. Either fixed convention works, but the columns of the first projection must follow the same ordering as the input blocks. For the vectors already used above, `кот` is $(1,0)$ and `пёс` is $(1,1)$. Chronological concatenation gives $(1,0,1,1)$. With projection row $(1,2,3,4)$, its pre-activation is 8. Reversing the two vector blocks gives $(1,1,1,0)$; the corresponding projection row must become $(3,4,1,2)$ to keep 8. Keeping the old row instead gives 6. When the same word occurs twice, both lookups select one parameter row. For the context `кот кот`, the projection is $(1+3)C_{\rm cat,0} +(2+4)C_{\rm cat,1}$. The gradient of this pre-activation with respect to the shared cat vector is therefore $(4,6)$, not two independently updated vectors. ```python import torch source_vectors = torch.zeros(8, 2, dtype=torch.float64) source_vectors[2] = torch.tensor([1., 0.]) # кот source_vectors[4] = torch.tensor([1., 1.]) # пёс source_vectors.requires_grad_() source_row = torch.tensor([1., 2., 3., 4.], dtype=torch.float64) chronological = source_vectors[[2, 4]].flatten() newest_first = source_vectors[[4, 2]].flatten() permuted_row = source_row.reshape(2, 2).flip(0).flatten() assert (chronological @ source_row).item() == 8 assert (newest_first @ permuted_row).item() == 8 assert (newest_first @ source_row).item() == 6 repeated = source_vectors[[2, 2]].flatten() lookup_gradient, = torch.autograd.grad(repeated @ source_row, source_vectors) expected_gradient = torch.zeros_like(source_vectors) expected_gradient[2] = torch.tensor([4., 6.]) torch.testing.assert_close(lookup_gradient, expected_gradient) ``` This calculation checks lookup sharing and block order. The complete nonlinear model, loss and optimizer are implemented below; it is not a reproduction of the paper's corpus-scale experiment.
